text.p: These are some of the leading stories in Israeli newspapers on Wednesday.
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
JERUSALEM POST
- U.S. expects regional thaw for Israel following Hebron redeployment.
- Jewish leaders want details of documents showing that Swedes sent Germany steel in return for Nazi gold.
- Hebron pact boosts tourism after a year in the doldrums. Lufthansa schedules additional 40 flights for spring.
- Israeli Comptroller Miriam Ben-Porat wants to impose sanctions on public-sector wage violators.
- Government: Bank Discount controlling share to be sold in 1997.
- Egyptian Ambassador to Israel: Hebron deal will boost Israeli-Arab trade.
- Migdal Insurance picks eight new executives. Assicurazioni Generali, Italy's largest insurer, recently signed agreement to acquire 40 percent of the group from Bank Leumi.
GLOBES
- Treasury officials against widening the moving band on the foreign currency exchange rate, effectively sharply re-evaluing shekel. Officials would even consider narrowing the band.
- Members of parliament won't give up on 6.9 percent salary rises but do put them off for six months until April 1.
- Bank Leumi: Expected devaluation in 1997 against the currency basket about 9 percent.
- Koor director-general Benny Gaon will next month go to Oman for negotiations on possible cooperation with local firms.
HAARETZ
- Foreign Minister David Levy exchanges messages with Syrian foreign minister, via high-ranking European. The two sides consider renewing negotiations.
- Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash tells Haaretz: "The missiles the Greek Cypriots bought from Russia threaten Israel too."
MAARIV
- Israel sounds alarm, saying there has been an erosion of the army's qualitative edge.
- Israeli army bans use of cellular phones in southern Lebanon for fear Hizbollah guerrillas are listening in.
YEDIOTH AHRONOTH
- Mossad says Syria has become the main threat because of its non-conventional missiles and delays in peace talks.
- Egyptian businessman buys shares in Israel's Koor in the United States. He is close to President Hosni Mubarak which suggests Cairo has given the green light for closer economic ties with Israel.
